entry.content:
Advertising

Netflix Swims Away With Ad-of-the-Week Honors

Plus: SickKids, Amazon, Xfinity, Verizon ... and the Clio Awards

by David Gianatasio
November 12, 2026
12:00 pm
2 min read
Share:

Here’s a rundown of the week’s best work, ranked by the Clios’ staff.

Bestie: Astronauts, Vampires and Adorable Amphibians Can’t Get Enough of Their Favorite Netflix Shows

Mother explores the intensity of fandom in three different settings: outer space, a vampire’s neighborhood and a fancy fish tank. All three spots absolutely slap, but the Bridgerton-besotted aquatic salamander swam (and walked!) into our hearts. From Netflix’s Brand Creative Studio and Iconoclast directors Vania Heymann and Gal Muggia. Read More and view the others here

2. Turning Donors Into Lifelines for SickKids Hospital

IV lines become symbols of life across time and space, aiding a young girl in her fight for survival. TBWA\Canada crafted this artful appeal with director Nico Perez Veiga from Iconoclast-Merchant. Powerhouse imagery helps it rank among the best health and wellness ads of the year. Read More

3. Amazon’s Christmas Epic Is About the Journey, Not So Much the Destination

The Beatles’ “Golden Slumbers” propels the retail kingpin’s short film, titled “Joy Delivered.” The track’s sleepy fairytale quality matches the snowy scenes from Amazon’s in-house team and Smuggler director Mark Molloy. Read More

4. In Xfinity’s Holiday Spot, John C. Reilly Wants You to Savor Every Moment—IRL, Not Online

The Oscar nominee plays a ghost in this Dickens riff about looking up from your damn screens and enjoying the holidays already. From Goodby Silverstein & Partners and O Positive director Jim Jenkins. Read More

5. Martin Short Elfs Himself for Verizon and We’re So There for It

Marty just dominates this Santa’s Workshop spoof, chewing scenery like he’s gobbling down an Xmas meal. From The Community and directors Jocelyn DeBoer and Dawn Luebbe. Read More

Special Mention: The Clio Awards Painted a Guy Gold in Its 2027 Call for Entries Campaign

We love our own work—deal with it! Srsly, this one’s good as gold. Beyond Studios exec and social-media star Cole Poska glitters in the central role. He showered after the shoot (probably). Read More

entry.title: For the Holidays, Apple Helps Make a Young Artist’s Dream Come True
entry.summary: Advertising For the Holidays, Apple Helps Make a Young Artist's Dream Come True Hebru Brantley created the artworks in a film directed by Melina Matsoukas by David Gianatasio November 12, 2026 8:45 am 3 min read Share: Some folks suffer for their art. But a MacBook Neo can give c
entry.content:
Advertising

For the Holidays, Apple Helps Make a Young Artist's Dream Come True

Hebru Brantley created the artworks in a film directed by Melina Matsoukas

by David Gianatasio
November 12, 2026
8:45 am
3 min read
Share:

Some folks suffer for their art. But a MacBook Neo can give creators the tools they need to realize their vision.

Running nearly 4 minutes, Apple’s 2026 holiday campaign tells such a story in sweet, starkly emotional terms. Developed by TBWA\Media Arts Lab, the film follows a young man’s quest for self-expression.

As a little kid and teenager, he flexes his talent by painting on his bedroom wall, skateboards and sneakers. His teachers and school friends just don’t understand—they even grow hostile at times. But his nurturing parents understand, providing support and gifts—both physical and emotional—to help him stay the course and find his way.

Strawberry Guy’s “Give Me a Dream” sets a dreamy-pop mood that fits the realism on screen from director Melina Matsoukas and cinematographer Bradford Young. Unlike many yuletide ads this year, many of which engage in flights of fancy and harness animation techniques, Apple keeps us grounded in the here and now, spinning a hopeful tale and summoning tears—but never leaning too hard on sentimentality.

Hebru Brantley created the various paintings and sculptures, adding a rich tactile language to the storyline, and the project hit close to home.

“Our experiences shape what we create. My mother saw the artist in me before I could see it in myself, and her belief gave me the confidence to explore that—which I’ll continue to honor,” he says in press materials

“That’s why this story is special to me. The right tools can help us unlock our creativity. For the young artist in the film, the MacBook Neo is also a reminder that his parents see the potential in him, and an invitation to reconnect with it.”

This BTS puts his efforts in perspective:

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Hello Apple (@helloapple)

It’s useful to consider the work in light of the stop-motion avalanche of Xmas ads this year. Those brands play up the painstaking craft behind their adverts to symbolize caring and quality in the age of AI. That’s all well and good, and such tactics probably resonate with many viewers who remain leery of generative advancements.

Here, Apple takes a somewhat different tack, tapping into raw emotions and youthful aspirations to sell laptops that put AI at our fingertips.

The tech giant trumpets its horn in a slightly different way, positioning itself as the source for innovations that can make users’ most cherished, hard-fought dreams a reality.

Related: “Amazon’s Christmas Epic Is all About the Journey, Not So Much the Destination”

entry.title: Amazon’s Christmas Epic Is About the Journey, Not So Much the Destination
entry.summary: Advertising Amazon's Christmas Epic Is About the Journey, Not So Much the Destination A sweet tale driven by the Beatles' 'Golden Slumbers' by Shahnaz Mahmud November 11, 2026 10:45 am 3 min read Share: Amazon focuses on the journey, not the destination, in its 2026 holiday spot
entry.content:
Advertising

Amazon's Christmas Epic Is About the Journey, Not So Much the Destination

A sweet tale driven by the Beatles' 'Golden Slumbers'

by Shahnaz Mahmud
November 11, 2026
10:45 am
3 min read
Share:

Amazon focuses on the journey, not the destination, in its 2026 holiday spot that dropped this week. The short film, titled “Joy Delivered,” runs two-and-a-half minutes and seeks to illustrate the spirit of giving.

New Zealand actress Kate Laidler, playing the character of Joy, sits glumly at the airport, her flight home canceled due to the raging snow outside. But her journey of kindness begins with an attendant who hands her his hat and helps her brave the storm.

Undeterred, she waits at a bus stop. A Planes, Trains and Automobiles scenario unfolds. The woman boards a bus, which hours later is parked in a snowbank. It’s here that Joy’s spirit of giving kicks in. She starts leaving labeled presents for her family with each person who has helped her on her way home. Each gets unwrapped in her presence—the Amazon boxes prominent under the paper and trim. 

Joy meets a cast of characters, including a donkey, a penguin and a reindeer, as she traverses a cliff and rides waves on the high seas. Finally, she reaches her mother’s home, which is decked out for the holidays.

“We always start by thinking about how customers are feeling heading into the season, and this year, the desire for community, generosity and kindness felt especially strong,” a brand rep tells Muse. “That idea of delivering joy is also at the heart of what Amazon does every holiday season: helping millions of customers find the perfect gift and making sure it arrives on time, at a great price, so they can spend more time with the people who matter most.”

The work was done in-house and directed by Mark Molloy via Smuggler. The Beatles’ “Golden Slumbers” serves as the soundtrack.

“Joy Delivered” was shot in New Zealand, against the backdrop of its dramatic and beautiful landscapes, adding scale to Joy’s journey home.

“It’s a story Amazon has a very natural role in telling,” the rep says. “The holidays are hectic, and our job is to make the season a little easier.”

As for the track selection, “We considered over a hundred songs before landing on ‘Golden Slumbers.’ We were able to secure the rights to Takes 1–3 and Take 17 from the Beatles’ original Abbey Road sessions, and blended them into a rendition.”

“Joy Delivered” will run across TV, digital, social and cinema through the holiday season.

entry.title: The U.K. Holiday Ads Keep Coming: Waitrose Joins Morrisons, John Lewis, Tesco and More
entry.summary: Advertising The U.K. Holiday Ads Keep Coming: Waitrose Joins Morrisons, John Lewis, Tesco and More Plus good cheer from Aldi, Asda, Argos, M&S and Sainsbury's by Shahnaz Mahmud November 11, 2026 9:00 am 5 min read Share: The holiday ad season is well underway in the U.K., with co
entry.content:
Advertising

The U.K. Holiday Ads Keep Coming: Waitrose Joins Morrisons, John Lewis, Tesco and More

Plus good cheer from Aldi, Asda, Argos, M&S and Sainsbury's

by Shahnaz Mahmud
November 11, 2026
9:00 am
5 min read
Share:

The holiday ad season is well underway in the U.K., with commercials dropping every day. Below, Muse looks at some of the notable entries so far. Classic themes abound, with brands leaning into familiar tropes and timeless tales to conjure the yuletide spirit. Updated: Nov. 11.

Waitrose, ‘The Perfect Gift 2’

Keira Knightley and Joe Wilkinson reprise their roles from Waitrose’s 2025 holiday rom-com in a fresh ad from Wonderhood Studios. Clocking in at nearly 6 minutes, “The Perfect Gift 2” finds Joe trying to win back Keria. and Of course only Beef Wellington will do, and that’s where Waitrose comes in. Molly Manners directed through Biscuit Filmworks.

Morrisons, ‘Christmas Made Just Right’

Morrisons reimagines Goldilocks and the Three Bears for the holiday season. Mama Bear and Papa Bear feverishly prepare (and grunt) for their Baby Bear’s visit, new girlfriend in tow. Mama puts up the tree and bakes a cake, while Papa visits a Morrisons supermarket to pick up dinner items. All is just right for this modern family—sort of—when Baby shows up with Goldilocks. At the table enjoying the spread, she fittingly tips over in her chair. Leo Burnett handled the creative.

Marks & Spencer, ‘The Home of Christmas’

Who needs a big white beard or red suit? James Norton plays Santa in decidedly contemporary casual style, bopping around for the holidays to a version of Belinda Carlyle’s “Heaven Is a Place on Earth” (performed by Katherine Jenkins). “I loved that this story takes such an iconic character and lets us see him differently,” Norton says. “He gets to experience Christmas like the rest of us, discovering that the real magic is in the food, traditions and moments we share with the people we love.” Lucy Punch stars as Mrs. Claus. Mother London developed the concept and Smuggler’s Shannon Murphy directed the 3-minute film.

John Lewis, ‘Don’t Give Up on Giving’

This marks the retailer’s 20th holiday campaign. Dame Kristin Scott Thomas shares the stage with a vintage Fisher-Price Snoopy-style toy. When Scott Thomas’ grandchildren arrive for the holidays, the kids aren’t impressed with the pooch. When she opts to put cash in an envelope to satisfy their holiday appetites, the doggo speaks up, telling her she can do better than that. Next, a magical neon pedicab whisks them away to a John Lewis store for a shopping spree. Back home, the kids are treated to a room filled with magical lights and disco balls. Naturally, they dance on with their grandma. A version of The Rolling Stones’ “You Can’t Always Get What You Want” adds a rocked-up vibe. Saatchi & Saatchi led the creative. 

Argos, ‘Tales of Argos Past’

Here, Argos riffs on Charles Dickens‘ A Christmas Carol. BAFTA-winning actor and comedian Richard Ayoade is visited by The Ghost of Christmas Presents and the Dinosaur of Argos Past. They transport him back to his childhood and, when they question what made him so gruff as an adult, Richard replies: “Life and despair.” They explain that, in his youth, he never got past the toy section, and then reveal all of the high-tech gadgets Argos sells in the here and now. At last, Richard comes to understand the error of his ways, leading to a happy Christmas Day. Declan Lowney of Merman directed, with T&P handling creative.

Sainsbury’s, ‘The Big Delivery’

The supermarket reimagines the world of Roald Dahl, focusing on The BFG—his 1982 novel featuring “The Big Friendly Giant.” Down with a bad cold, The BFG decides to forgo Christmas. But his human friends Annie and Fred deliver him a holiday feast. The spot, which uses live action and animation, puts the friends in peril en route in their car. Antics with a giant mouse, a king-sized cheese platter and Brussels sprouts follow. When they arrive safely, they proclaim: “No one should miss Christmas!” The push was created by New Commercial Arts, while Rogue Films handled production. Electric Theatre Collective oversaw visual effects. 

Tesco, ‘Because the Wrong Address’

The supermarket chain pulls at the heartstrings with a story about a long-ago friendship that went awry. Lizzie had a food delivery order sent to a previous address. Goodhearted Polly offers to meet her halfway. It becomes clear they were friends in the past, but the relationship soured. Lizzie gives an abrupt thanks and waves Polly off, but her car won’t start. Polly comes to the rescue and drives her old friend home. Will the tale end happily? Perhaps around a dinner table set with goodies from Tesco. Will it!? BBH London created the work. 

Asda, ‘All of Christmas at Asda Price. BOOM!’

The grocer opts for a highly stylized Christmas epic, showcasing food, home decor and more. The tale morphs from a family gathering at the dinner table—with Asda low-low price tags near some of the items—to a party featuring the mum riding on a giant Christmas cracker among dancing toy soldiers. BOOM! indeed. From Lucky Generals.

Aldi, Teaser: ‘The Search for Cauli-Dog’

The grocer carries beloved characters forward for its 2026 ad offer. Here, we get a tease of things to come. Aldi puts Kevin the Carrot at the center once again. He and his daughter Chantenay are putting up missing posters for their Cauli-Dog. Clues will trickle in from Aldi, keeping the suspense going. McCann Manchester helped develop the campaign.

entry.title: Carl’s Jr. Suits Up for a ‘Fancy Pants’ Romp
entry.summary: Advertising Carl's Jr. Suits Up for a 'Fancy Pants' Romp Thanks to AI, outrageous styles fit Bert Kreischer every time by David Gianatasio November 10, 2026 12:00 pm 2 min read Share: Dressing comic Bert Kreischer in outlandish piano-pants with working keyboards and Mozart clingi
entry.content:
Advertising

Carl's Jr. Suits Up for a 'Fancy Pants' Romp

Thanks to AI, outrageous styles fit Bert Kreischer every time

by David Gianatasio
November 10, 2026
12:00 pm
2 min read
Share:

Dressing comic Bert Kreischer in outlandish piano-pants with working keyboards and Mozart clinging to his leg—surely, THAT’S what AI was invented for!

And it delivers funny fashions in funny fashion to introduce Carl Jr.’s Angus Steakhouse Burger. That 1/3-pound charbroiled beef x melty Swiss treat is so “fancy,” Bert needs elaborate pants to drop in for a bite.

Be careful, dude. You don’t want to drip bistro sauce all over those 3000-carat Capris.

“We needed to launch a new premium burger, so we knew showing lots of mouthwatering food footage would be a must,” says Eric Kallman, CCO at Erich & Kallman, which developed the campaign. “So, we got excited when we found a creative construct that allowed us to show mostly burger footage while popping away quickly to Bert for fun moments.”

Why cast Bert specifically?

“Carl’s customers lean male and younger, and Bert is a constant in their feeds these days,” Kallman explains. “He’s pretty universally loved and we knew he would be a great choice to pull off the gag. Also, it turns out he’s an actual Carl’s Jr fan, and he actually chose this project over one from a competitor.”

OK, now tell us all about the pants!

“Most were AI generated, so at the shoot Bert had to wear pants made out of foam that were roughly the same size and shape, so his movements would be true to the pants that we created in post.”

But a few of them were real, like the “Plantaloons” made of hedges, “which were really annoying for Bert to wear.”

Some never made the cut, like a pair covered in 100s of bow ties. “I think Bert took those home with him, along with Capris,” Kallman says.

Zachary Johnson and Jeffrey Max, aka Fatal Farm, directed through product house Gravy.

This marks an AI trifecta for Carl’s in recent months, following these two fun outings:

Carl’s Jr. Cooks Up Gladiator vs. Clown Combat in the Colosseum

Carl’s Jr. Sends in the Paris Hilton AI Clones

entry.summary: Advertising Levi's Yeti Roars Atop the Week's Best Campaigns With Midi Health, e.l.f. Beauty, Visit Iceland and Columbia Sportswear by David Gianatasio November 5, 2026 12:00 pm 2 min read Share: This week’s best work, ranked by the Clios’ staff, features two impressive stop-moti
entry.content:
Advertising

Levi's Yeti Roars Atop the Week's Best Campaigns

With Midi Health, e.l.f. Beauty, Visit Iceland and Columbia Sportswear

by David Gianatasio
November 5, 2026
12:00 pm
2 min read
Share:

This week’s best work, ranked by the Clios’ staff, features two impressive stop-motion campaigns and other excellent efforts. But nothing beats a Yeti, especially for the festive season.

Bestie: A Claymation Yeti Stomps Through Levi’s Holiday Campaign

This beast gets a sweet character arc. He starts out gruesome and destructive. Will he cough up some bucks for smashing through the cabin wall? Probably not. But a Levi’s sweater puts him in the mellowest yuletide mood. Superb Claymation stylings from Blinkink. Read More

2. Top Comics Michelle Buteau, Jessica Kirson and More Roast Menopause for Midi Health

The notion of “roasting’ menopause itself might sound like a stretch. But these performers deliver a show that’s hilarious and on point. If you want to start a cultural convo about potentially touchy topics, laughter can provide the best way in. Read More

3. Alan Cumming Narrates e.l.f.’s Animated Holiday Spot

The Shadow agency and Apartment D director Cami Kwan help the brand convey a heartfelt message that packs more whimsical imagery than you can fit beneath a tree. Yet, it also feels grounded in reality, with Alan Cumming working his Scottish pipes for a warm and winning V.O. Read More

4. Who Needs AI Notetakers? Visit Iceland Offers ‘Knittakers’ Instead

Real Icelanders from across the Nordic nation will take your place on video calls and knit brief summaries for your pleasure. M+C Saatchi developed the initiative, which stitches tech, old-school craft and odd humor into an attractive tapestry. Or maybe a sweater. Read More

5. Columbia Sportswear’s Bunker Helps You Survive the Apocalypse in Rugged Style

And the prize for best performance by a CEO in a bunker goes to Columbia’s Tim Boyle. Who wouldn’t want a 40 ft. x 8 ft. steel container brimming with gear and grub buried in their backyard? From Adam&Eve\TBWA and Smuggler director Benji Weinstein. Read More

entry.summary: Advertising Chewy Joins the Stop-Motion Avalanche Is this the doggone cutest holiday campaign of the year? (Spoiler: probably) by David Gianatasio November 4, 2026 9:15 am 4 min read Share: And now for something completely different: A stop-motion holiday campaign. The parade of
entry.content:
Advertising

Chewy Joins the Stop-Motion Avalanche

Is this the doggone cutest holiday campaign of the year? (Spoiler: probably)

by David Gianatasio
November 4, 2026
9:15 am
4 min read
Share:

And now for something completely different: A stop-motion holiday campaign.

The parade of animated fare continues with Chewy joining e.l.f. and Levi’s via three shorts developed with Starburns and director David Shafei.

Unlike the other two brands, Chewy blends stop motion and live action to bridge the gap between real-life and a snowy fantasy world. Its iconic blue delivery box serves as a portal, natch. Ratcheting up the cuteness, real doggos and their puppet doppelgängers appear.

The pooches, snowmen, mice, pine trees, a penguin, a cat and more were handcrafted from needle-wool over wire armatures. Their faces and body language are sweet and expressive. Some might find the approach too adorbs for its own good. But such grumps deserve coal in their stockings.

Next, the brand hypes its “Chewy Claus” program that helps support pet adoptions at participating shelters nationwide:

Wisely, these vignettes tell simple tales. They’re imminently snackable, but packed with great details that merit repeat viewings.

Yes, there’s a risk of stop-burnout this festive season—and we’re just a few days into November. Still, these efforts have all been top-notch so far. And Chewy’s initiative feels nostalgic without getting too Rankin-Bassy. Which is to say it’s pleasingly familiar but also stands out, thanks in large part to the puppetry replacing Claymation.

Also of note: the trend of brands self-consciously eschewing AI in favor of traditional creative techniques. This approach has become synonymous with dedication to craft, conveying notions of human attention to detail and quality. Fair enough. But AI’s here to stay; it’s one more tool in adland’s kit. One wonders how long marketers—which automate various processes left and right—will continue to trumpet their artisanal leanings before the point becomes moot (or even starts to feel regressive).

“We want to capture a little bit of what pets feel when they see a Chewy box,” Shafei explains in the BTS reel below. “We’re trying to blend the magic of the holiday with the magic of our pets. And I just can’t think of a better way to bring that through than stop-motion animation.”

Here, Muse chats with Chewy chief brand officer Melissa Bell about the strategy:

What was the inspo here?

The idea stems from imagining what a dream holiday world would look like to our pets. For five years, Chewy Claus has brought magic to pets during the holidays by delivering gifts and fulfilling big and small wishes. A Santa Claus for pets was something they could only dream of before Chewy Claus existed and these TV spots delve deeper into what else our pets dream of for the holidays. Whether that’s a forever home, a new cozy bed, their favorite treats or playing in the snow with their furry best friends.

Who is the target audience—current customers? Looking for new ones?

The target is always pet parents. When they see these ads, we want them to experience the nostalgia and joy from the holiday classics we know and love, but through their pet’ eyes and remember Chewy has everything they need to make their pets’ holiday season special.

No AI anywhere—right?

Correct. Every detail was thoughtfully crafted by professional artists and craftspeople, with no AI-generated visuals used in the production. Our customers have always appreciated the personal, one-of-a-kind touches they receive from Chewy, whether it’s receiving a hand-painted pet portrait, a heartfelt birthday card or a condolence gift after losing a pet. We believe in the power of connecting through real, human interactions.

Lots of cute animated Xmas ads—this year more than ever. Why will yours stand out?

We have some pretty cute talent in our spots! Before Graham was the star of our Chewy Claus spot, he was an actual rescue dog looking for a family. And the other puppets are inspired by real animals as well. We believe combining the real pets with the Chewy dream world version of themselves makes the creative not only adorable, but also memorable.

Columbia Sportswear's Bunker Helps You Survive the Apocalypse in Rugged Style

It's a 'Don't Panic Room.' So try to maintain your composure

by David Gianatasio
October 30, 2026
10:00 am
4 min read
Share:

If civilization suddenly implodes, you’ll want to rock gear with a spiffy logo when you emerge into the post-apocalyptic wilderness.

To that end, Columbia Sportswear steps up to the end-times challenge with a “Don’t Panic Room” contest that features a steel shipping container tricked out like a survivalist’s kitschy, branded dream. Along with loads of Columbia jackets, they packed tools, utensils, cots, a chemical toilet and tins of food (including “Some Kind of Meat”) into the 40 ft. x 8 ft. space. It won’t sit rusting in your back yard or driveway, because Columbia will pay for you to actually bury the thing.

You get a robo-dog for companionship, too. Perhaps it can parlay with near-future kill-bots annihilating any humans that remain. Good boy!

CEO Tim Boyle stars in an amusing promo below from Adam&Eve\TBWA and Smuggler director Benji Weinstein.

“Since the beginning of time, people have predicted the end of the world,” he says. “I don’t really buy into all that stuff. But since Columbia protects helps protect you from nature’s worst, we figure, ‘Better safe than sorry.'”

“Those tech bros already have their bunkers,” Boyle continues. “But they don’t have the skills to survive outdoors. Try starting a campfire with crypto. Or fly-fishing with microchips. Good luck with that.”

The competition invites folks to send videos displaying their survival skills for a chance to win. That grounds the stunt in Columbia’s consumer community, acknowledging their fans’ dedication to hiking, foraging, navigation and all manner of sweaty wilderness activities.

“We want to reward the real survivalists and outdoors people who appreciate what Mother Nature has to offer,” says brand marketing chief Matt Sutton.

Columbia accepts entries through Nov. 24. In addition to the hero clip, the initiative features Silicon Valley billboards and influencer support.

Below, agency creative William Cottam and James Crosby break down the strategy.

What was the inspo here?

We kept seeing stories about Silicon Valley tech bros building themselves elaborate bunkers. Which got us thinking, what’s the point of having a bunker if you don’t have the skills to survive outside it? So we thought it’d be funny if Columbia gave one away to someone who actually knows what they’re doing. You know, someone who could actually keep humanity going.

Why a survival room specifically?

Columbia has been engineering gear to protect people from Mother Nature for nearly 90 years. So building something to protect you from absolutely everything felt like a pretty natural, if slightly ridiculous, extension of that. It’s “Engineered for Whatever” taken to its logical extreme. Even if that extreme is an ice age, a meteor taking out the power grid or whatever sends us all running for the hills.

Who’s the target audience and why will it appeal to them?

Anyone who loves the outdoors and reckons they could survive with more than a smartphone and a decent Wi-Fi connection. We wanted to celebrate genuine outdoor skills rather than the size of someone’s bank account. And, frankly, who wouldn’t want to win a bunker?

I like how this transcends ad creative. It feels so tactile and real.

That’s what we love about it, too. We didn’t want to just make an ad about a bunker. We wanted to actually build the bloody thing. There’s something wonderfully ridiculous about creating a fully functioning 40-foot survival bunker, filling it with Columbia gear and delivering it to someone’s home. Columbia’s even agreed to give the winner $35,000 to help bury the thing underground. I mean, that’s commitment. Let’s just hope the winner has a spare 8 ft. x 40 ft. patch of land lying around.

Nice CEO performance, too.

Tim comes to the table with his own ideas, like the dog pooping bolts at the end. That was all him. And he was more than happy to get behind the wheel of a semi-truck too. He genuinely has fun with it all, which makes our jobs a lot easier.
